2026 BASE PROSPECTUS                                                                                                             19 May 2026

Zurich Insurance Company Ltd
(incorporated with limited liability in Switzerland)
Zurich Finance (Australia) Limited
Zurich Finance (Ireland) DAC
(incorporated with limited liability in Ireland)
Zurich Finance (Ireland) II DAC
(incorporated with limited liability in Ireland)
Zurich Holding Company of America, Inc.
(incorporated with limited liability in the United States of America)
irrevocably guaranteed, in the case of Notes issued by Zurich Finance (Australia) Limited, Zurich Finance (Ireland)
DAC, Zurich Finance (Ireland) II DAC and Zurich Holding Company of America, Inc. by
Zurich Insurance Company Ltd
USD18,000,000,000
Euro Medium Term Note Programme
Under this USD18,000,000,000 Euro Medium Term Note Programme (the “Programme”), Zurich Finance (Australia) Limited (“ZF (Australia)”),
Zurich Finance (Ireland) DAC (“ZF (Ireland)”), Zurich Finance (Ireland) II DAC (“ZF (Ireland) II”), Zurich Holding Company of America, Inc.
(“ZHCA”) and Zurich Insurance Company Ltd (“ZIC”, and together with ZF (Australia), ZF (Ireland), ZF (Ireland) II and ZHCA, the “Issuers”
and each, an “Issuer”) may from time to time (subject to the terms and conditions set out herein) issue (i) in relation to ZIC, ZF (Australia), ZF
(Ireland) and ZHCA only, Senior Notes and (ii) in relation to ZIC and ZF (Ireland) II only, Subordinated Notes (each as defined below and together
the “Notes”) denominated in any currency agreed between the relevant Issuer and the relevant Dealer (as defined below). Issues of Notes under the
Programme by ZF (Australia), ZF (Ireland), ZF (Ireland) II and ZHCA will be guaranteed as provided herein as to payments of principal, interest
and additional amounts by ZIC (in such capacity, the “Guarantor”).
“Guaranteed Subordinated Notes” means Notes issued by ZF (Ireland) II under the Programme pursuant to the Guaranteed Subordinated Notes
Conditions (which rank as set out in Condition 3(a) of the Guaranteed Subordinated Notes Conditions and have the benefit of the ZIC Subordinated
Guarantee), as specified in the applicable Pricing Supplement.
“Guaranteed Subordinated Notes Conditions” means the terms and conditions of the Subordinated Notes where the Issuer is ZF (Ireland) II.
“Senior Notes” means Notes issued by ZIC, ZF (Australia), ZF (Ireland) or ZHCA under the Programme pursuant to the Senior Notes Conditions
(which rank as set out in Condition 3 of the Senior Notes Conditions and, in the case of any Senior Notes issued by ZF (Australia), ZF (Ireland) or
ZHCA, which have the benefit of the ZIC Senior Guarantee).
“Senior Notes Conditions” means the terms and conditions of the Senior Notes.
“Subordinated Notes” means either (i) ZIC Subordinated Notes or (ii) Guaranteed Subordinated Notes.
“ZIC Senior Guarantee” means the guarantee provided by ZIC in relation to any issue of Senior Notes issued by ZF (Australia), ZF (Ireland) or
ZHCA, the form of which is set out herein (see “Form of ZIC Senior Guarantee”).
“ZIC Subordinated Guarantee” means the guarantee provided by ZIC in relation to any issue of Subordinated Notes issued by ZF (Ireland) II,
the form of which is set out herein (see “Form of ZIC Subordinated Guarantee”).
“ZIC Subordinated Notes” means Notes issued by ZIC under the Programme pursuant to the ZIC Subordinated Notes Conditions (which rank as
set out in Condition 3(a) of the ZIC Subordinated Notes Conditions), as specified in the applicable Pricing Supplement.
“ZIC Subordinated Notes Conditions” means the terms and conditions of the Subordinated Notes issued by ZIC.
The Notes may be issued on a continuous basis to one or more of the Dealers below and any additional Dealer appointed under the Programme
from time to time, which appointments may be for a specific issue or on an ongoing basis (each a “Dealer” and together the “Dealers”). References
in this Base Prospectus to the “relevant Dealer” shall, in the case of an issue of Notes being (or intended to be) subscribed by more than one
Dealer, be to all Dealers agreeing to purchase such Notes. References in this Base Prospectus to the “relevant Issuer” shall, in the case of any issue
of Notes, be to the Issuer which has agreed to issue such Notes.
This Base Prospectus does not comprise a prospectus or a base prospectus for the purposes of Regulation (EU) 2017/1129 (the “Prospectus
Regulation”). This Base Prospectus has been prepared solely in order to allow Notes to be offered in circumstances which do not impose
an obligation on the Issuers or any Dealer to publish or supplement a prospectus under the Prospectus Regulation. No prospectus is
required in accordance with the Prospectus Regulation in relation to offers of Notes under this Base Prospectus.
This Base Prospectus may only be used for the purposes for which it has been published.
This Base Prospectus constitutes a prospectus for the purposes of Part IV of the Luxembourg Law of 16 July 2019 relating to prospectuses for
securities. Application has been made for the Notes to be admitted to listing on the Official List of the Luxembourg Stock Exchange (the “Official
List”) and to trading on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange’s Euro MTF Market (the “Euro MTF Market”). References in this Base Prospectus to
Notes being listed (and all related references) shall mean that such Notes have been admitted to trading on the Euro MTF Market and have been
listed on the Official List. The Euro MTF Market is not a regulated market for the purposes of Directive 2014/65/EU (as amended, “MiFID II”).
This Base Prospectus has not been approved by and will not be submitted for approval to the Commission de surveillance du secteur financier of
Luxembourg.

As specified in the applicable Pricing Supplement, an issue of Notes may or may not be listed or admitted to trading, as the case may be, on the
Luxembourg Stock Exchange and/or any other stock exchange(s), market(s) or quotation system(s) as may be agreed between the relevant Issuer
and the relevant Dealer(s).
With respect to a particular Series (as defined on page iii) of Notes issued in registered form (“Registered Notes”), the Registered Notes of each
Tranche (as defined on page iii) of such Series will be sold outside the United States of America (the “United States” or “U.S.”) in reliance on
Regulation S under the United States Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “U.S. Securities Act”). Such Notes will be represented by a global
note in registered form, without interest coupons (a “Reg. S Global Note”), which will be registered in the name of Citivic Nominees Limited as
nominee for, and will be deposited with Citibank, N.A., as common depositary for, and in respect of interests held through, Euroclear Bank SA/NV
(“Euroclear”) and Clearstream Banking S.A. (“Clearstream”). If a Reg. S Global Note is held under the New Safekeeping Structure (the “NSS”),
the Reg. S Global Note will be delivered on or prior to the original issue date of the relevant Tranche to a common safekeeper (the “Common
Safekeeper”) for Euroclear and Clearstream. Prior to expiry of the period that ends 40 days after completion of the distribution of each Tranche of
Notes (the “distribution compliance period”), beneficial interests in the Reg. S Global Note may not be offered or sold to, or for the account or
benefit of, a U.S. person (as defined in Regulation S under the U.S. Securities Act), and may not be held otherwise than through Euroclear and
Clearstream. Registered Notes in individual form will be issued in exchange for interests in the Reg. S Global Note upon compliance with the
procedures for exchange as described in “Description of Notes in Global Form” below in the limited circumstances described in the applicable
Pricing Supplement. Registered Notes in individual registered form from the date of issue may also be sold outside the United States in reliance on
Regulation S under the U.S. Securities Act.
Each Tranche of Notes issued in bearer form (“Bearer Notes”) (other than a Tranche of Listed Swiss Franc Notes, as to which see “Description of
Notes in Global Form”) will initially be represented by a temporary bearer global Note (a “Temporary Global Note”) or, if so specified in the
applicable Pricing Supplement, a permanent Global Note (a “Permanent Global Note”, together with the Temporary Global Note, the “Bearer
Global Notes”) which if the Bearer Global Notes are not intended to be issued in new global note (“New Global Note” or “NGN”) form, will be
deposited on or around the relevant issue date with a common depositary (the “Common Depositary”) for Euroclear and Clearstream, and if the
Bearer Global Notes are intended to be issued in NGN form, will be deposited on or around the relevant issue date with a Common Safekeeper for
Euroclear and Clearstream. Beneficial interests in a Temporary Global Note will be exchangeable for either beneficial interests in a Permanent
Global Note or Definitive Bearer Notes upon certification as to non-U.S. beneficial ownership as required by U.S. Treasury Regulations and
thereafter any Permanent Global Note may be exchanged for Definitive Bearer Notes in the circumstances described in the applicable Pricing
Supplement, in each case in accordance with the procedures described in “Description of Notes in Global Form” below. All Bearer Notes issued
by ZHCA will be issued so as to be in registered form for U.S. federal income tax purposes.
Prospective investors should have regard to the factors described under the section headed “Risk Factors” in this Base Prospectus.

Notes will be issued in series (each a “Series”) having one or more issue dates and on terms otherwise identical
(or identical other than in respect of the first payment of interest), the Notes of each Series being intended to be
interchangeable with all other Notes of that Series. Each Series may be issued in tranches (each a “Tranche”)
on different issue dates.

Notice of the aggregate nominal amount of Notes, interest (if any) payable in respect of Notes, the issue price
of Notes and any other terms and conditions not contained herein which are applicable to each Tranche of Notes
will be set out in the pricing supplement (the “applicable Pricing Supplement” or “relevant Pricing
Supplement”) which, with respect to Notes to be listed on a stock exchange, will be delivered to the stock
exchange on or before the date of issue of the Notes of such Tranche. Notes that will not be admitted to listing,
trading and/or quotation by any listing authority, stock exchange and/or quotation system may also be issued
pursuant to the Programme by any of the Issuers.

No person is or has been authorised to give any information or to make any representation not contained in or

Neither this Base Prospectus nor any other information supplied in connection with the Programme or any

constitute an offer by or on behalf of any Issuer, the Trustee, the Agents or any of the Dealers to any person to
subscribe for or to purchase any Notes.

The delivery of this Base Prospectus does not at any time imply that the information contained herein

condition or affairs of the Issuers during the life of the Programme. Investors should review, inter alia, the most
recently published audited annual financial statements and, if published later, the most recently published
interim financial statements (if any) of the relevant Issuer and ZIC (where ZIC is not the relevant Issuer) when
deciding whether or not to purchase any Notes.

The Pricing Supplement in respect of any Notes may include a legend entitled “MiFID II Product Governance”

“distributor”) should take into consideration the target market assessment; however, a distributor subject to

A determination will be made in relation to each issue of Notes about whether, for the purpose of the MiFID II
Product Governance rules under EU Delegated Directive 2017/593 (the “MiFID II Product Governance
Rules”), any Dealer subscribing for any Notes is a manufacturer in respect of such Notes, but otherwise neither

The Pricing Supplement in respect of any Notes may include a legend entitled “UK MiFIR Product

determining appropriate distribution channels.

A determination will be made in relation to each issue of Notes about whether, for the purpose of the UK MiFIR
Product Governance Rules, any Dealer subscribing for any Notes is a manufacturer in respect of such Notes,

EU BENCHMARKS REGULATION: Interest and/or other amounts payable under the Notes may be calculated
by reference to certain reference rates. Any such reference rate may constitute a benchmark for the purposes of
Regulation (EU) 2016/1011 (as amended, the “EU Benchmarks Regulation”). If any such reference rate does
constitute such a benchmark, the applicable Pricing Supplement will indicate whether or not the benchmark is
provided by an administrator included in the register of administrators and benchmarks established and
maintained by the European Securities and Markets Authority (“ESMA”) pursuant to Article 36 of the EU
Benchmarks Regulation. The registration status of any administrator under the EU Benchmarks Regulation is
a matter of public record and, save where required by applicable law, the relevant Issuer does not intend to
update the relevant Pricing Supplement to reflect any change in the registration status of the administrator.

If the relevant Pricing Supplement in respect of any Notes includes a legend entitled “Prohibition of Sales to
EEA Retail Investors”, the Notes are not intended to be offered, sold or otherwise made available to and should
not be offered, sold or otherwise made available to any retail investor in the European Economic Area (“EEA”).
For these purposes, a retail investor means a person who is one (or more) of: (i) a retail client as defined in point
(11) of Article 4(1) of MiFID II; (ii) a customer within the meaning of Directive (EU) 2016/97, where that
customer would not qualify as a professional client as defined in point (10) of Article 4(1) of MiFID II; or (iii)
not a qualified investor as defined in the Prospectus Regulation. Consequently, no key information document
required by Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014 (as amended, the “PRIIPs Regulation”) for offering or selling the
Notes or otherwise making them available to retail investors in the EEA has been prepared and therefore offering
or selling the Notes or otherwise making them available to any retail investor in the EEA may be unlawful under
the PRIIPs Regulation.

If the relevant Pricing Supplement in respect of any Notes includes a legend entitled “Prohibition of Sales to
UK Retail Investors”, the Notes are not intended to be offered, sold, distributed or otherwise made available to
and should not be offered, sold, distributed or otherwise made available to any retail investor in the United
Kingdom (“UK”). For these purposes, a retail investor means a person who is either one (or both) of the
following: (i) not a professional client, as defined in point (8) of Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) No 600/2014
as it forms part of domestic law by virtue of the EUWA; or (ii) not a qualified investor as defined in paragraph
15 of Schedule 1 to the Public Offers and Admissions to Trading Regulations 2024 (the “POATRs”).
Consequently, no disclosure document required by the FCA Product Disclosure Sourcebook (“DISC”) for
offering, selling or distributing the Notes or otherwise making them available to retail investors in the UK has
been prepared and therefore offering, selling or distributing the Notes or otherwise making them available to
any retail investor in the UK may be unlawful under the DISC and the Consumer Composite Investments
(Designated Activities) Regulations 2024.

The Notes have not been and will not be registered under the U.S. Securities Act or with any securities
regulatory authority of any state or other jurisdiction of the United States and the Notes may include bearer
Notes that are subject to U.S. tax law requirements. Notes may not be offered, sold or delivered within the
United States or to, or for the account or benefit of, U.S. persons (as defined in Regulation S under the U.S.
Securities Act) except in accordance with Regulation S under the U.S. Securities Act or pursuant to an
exemption from the registration requirements of the U.S. Securities Act (see “Subscription and Sale” below)
and hedging transactions involving the Notes may not be conducted unless in compliance with the U.S.
Securities Act.

This Base Prospectus is provided for the purpose of giving information with regard to the Issuers, the Guarantor
and the Notes which, according to the particular nature of the Issuers, the Guarantor and the Notes, is necessary
to enable investors to make an informed assessment of the assets and liabilities, financial position, profit and

disclosure document within the meaning of section 9 of the Corporations Act 2001 of Australia, as amended
(“Corporations Act”), or a product disclosure statement for the purposes of Chapter 7 of the Corporations Act.
No action has been taken that would permit a public offering of the Notes in Australia. In particular, this Base
Prospectus has not been, and will not be, lodged or registered with the Australian Securities and Investments
Commission (“ASIC”). Notes may not be offered for sale nor may applications for the sale or purchase of any
Notes be invited in Australia (including an offer or invitation that is received by a person in Australia) and
neither this Base Prospectus, any pricing supplement, nor any advertisement or other offering material relating
to the Notes may be distributed or published in Australia unless (i) (A) the aggregate amount payable on
acceptance of the offer by each offeree or invitee for the Notes is a minimum amount (disregarding amounts, if
any, lent by the person offering the Notes or its associates) of A$500,000 (or its equivalent in another currency),
or (B) the offer or invitation is otherwise an offer or invitation for which no disclosure is required to be made
under Part 6D.2 or Chapter 7 of the Corporations Act, (ii) the offer, invitation or distribution complies with all
applicable laws and regulations relating to the offer, sale and resale of the Notes in the jurisdiction in which
such offer, sale and resale occurs, and (iii) such action does not require any document to be lodged with ASIC.

Citigroup Global Markets Limited is incorporated in the United Kingdom and is authorised in the United

Sale” below).

in the EEA and registered under Regulation (EC) No 1060/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council
of 16 September 2009 on credit rating agencies, as amended (the “EU CRA Regulation”). S&P is not

Tranches of Notes may be rated or unrated. Where a Tranche of Notes is rated, the applicable rating(s) will be
specified in the relevant Pricing Supplement. Whether or not each credit rating applied for in relation to a
relevant Tranche of Notes will be issued by a credit rating agency established in the European Union and
registered under the EU CRA Regulation will be disclosed in the relevant Pricing Supplement. In general, EU
regulated investors are restricted under the EU CRA Regulation from using credit ratings for regulatory
purposes unless such ratings are issued by a credit rating agency established in the EU and registered under the

restriction will also apply in the case of credit ratings issued by non-EU credit rating agencies, unless the
relevant credit ratings are endorsed by an EU-registered credit rating agency or the relevant non-EU rating
agency is certified in accordance with the EU CRA Regulation (and such endorsement action or certification,
as the case may be, has not been withdrawn or suspended, subject to transitional provisions that apply in certain
circumstances). In general, UK regulated investors are restricted under the UK CRA Regulation from using

pending. Such general restriction will also apply in the case of credit ratings issued by non-UK credit rating
agencies, unless the relevant credit ratings are endorsed by a UK-registered credit rating agency or the relevant
non-UK rating agency is certified in accordance with the UK CRA Regulation (and such endorsement action or
certification, as the case may be, has not been withdrawn or suspended, subject to transitional provisions that
apply in certain circumstances). A rating is not a recommendation to buy, sell or hold Notes and may be subject
to suspension, change or withdrawal at any time by the assigning rating agency.

STABILISATION MAY NOT NECESSARILY OCCUR. ANY STABILISATION ACTION MAY BEGIN

SUPPLEMENT OF THE OFFER OF THE RELEVANT TRANCHE OF NOTES IS MADE AND, IF

DAYS AFTER THE ISSUE DATE OF THE RELEVANT TRANCHE OF NOTES AND 60 DAYS AFTER

RISKS RELATING TO THE ISSUERS AND THE ZIC GROUP

Insurance Risk
The prospects and the profitability of ZIC and its subsidiaries (collectively the “ZIC Group”) are, among other
things, subject to insurance risks in its primary businesses. Insurance risk is the risk of deviation from what is
expected in the timing, frequency or severity of insured events, which may lead to loss, including adverse
change in the value of insurance liabilities. This may result from inherent uncertainty of insured events or losses,
inadequate or ineffective underwriting or accumulation management, inappropriate product development,
pricing, claims management, reserving or reinsurance. The profitability of insurance business is also susceptible
to business risk in the form of unexpected changes in expenses, policyholders’ behaviour and fluctuations in
new business volumes.

In the ZIC Group’s Property and Casualty business segment, insurance risks consist mainly of premium and
reserve risks, but also include catastrophe and business risks. These risks reflect uncertainties in the frequency
of the occurrence of the insured events and the severity of the resulting claims. In the ZIC Group’s Life
insurance business segment, the major insurance risks are associated with biometric factors, such as mortality
risk, longevity risk and morbidity risk. Policyholder behaviour risk (e.g., surrender risk) is also a major risk
driver for Life insurance business. It should be noted that there could be an accumulation of losses across Life
insurance and Property and Casualty business segments (e.g., property damage and loss of lives in the same
earthquake). Any such losses could have a material adverse effect on the ZIC Group’s results of operations and
financial condition.

Insurance Risk Relating to Property and Casualty Business Segment
Property and Casualty insurance risk arises from coverage provided for motor, property, liability, special lines
and worker injury. It comprises premium and reserve risk, catastrophe risk, and business risk. Premium and
reserve risk covers uncertainties in the frequency of the occurrence of the insured events as well as in the
severity of the resulting claims. Catastrophe risk predominantly relates to uncertainty around natural
catastrophes. Business risk predominantly relates to unexpected increases in the expenses relating to claims
handling, underwriting, and administration.

Premium and Reserve Risk
Property and Casualty insurance reserves are regularly estimated, reviewed and monitored by actuaries at local,
regional and ZIC Group levels. To arrive at their reserve estimates, the ZIC Group’s actuaries take into
consideration, among other things, the latest information regarding loss payments, as well as related trends and

patterns, and apply actuarial judgment to the available information. Incorrect or incomplete information and/or
actuarial judgment may result in insufficient reserves to cover actual liabilities and/or in the underwriting of
unprofitable business.

There is no guarantee that reserves will be sufficient to cover actual losses, as claims can develop adversely
over time. This risk is particularly significant in respect of long tail exposures, where claims are often settled
long after the policy’s exposure period has ended. Examples include worker injury and liability contracts, as
well as losses related to toxic tort (e.g., asbestos), environmental pollution and medical malpractice. Changes
in legislation or regulations with retroactive effect, developments in legal precedents which favour plaintiffs,
as well as increases in the cost or scope of healthcare or repairs, along with other inflationary-driven increases
in factors such as wages, may result in a requirement to increase reserves in response to higher estimates of
claim levels. See “—Market Risks—Inflation Risk”.

If the ZIC Group has insufficient reserves to cover actual losses or is required to increase reserves in response
to higher estimates of claim levels, this may have an adverse effect on the ZIC Group’s business, financial
condition and results of operations.

Catastrophe Risk
As part of its Property and Casualty business, the ZIC Group is also exposed to potentially large losses from
natural catastrophes such as hurricanes, floods, windstorms, earthquakes, tornadoes, fires, severe hail and severe
winter weather. Such events are inherently unpredictable in terms of both their frequency and severity,
particularly as the effects of climate change may render estimates based on historical data less reliable as an
indicator of potential future exposures. See “—Other Risks Relating to the ZIC Group’s Business and
Operations—Climate Change Risk”.

While these events are inherently unpredictable, there are also several challenges to modelling them. There is a
risk that the selection of models may be inappropriate for the intended risk and/or that the complexity of the
models may lead to incorrect interpretations of their results. The input data to the models may also contribute
to the risk of underestimating losses from natural catastrophes, because it may be incomplete or lacking in
quality. Furthermore, modelling may fail to incorporate trends and/or climate change into the models (e.g.,
changing vulnerabilities or feedback between physical and transition climate risks). See further “—Other Risks
Relating to the ZIC Group’s Business and Operations—Climate Change Risk”.

The occurrence of natural catastrophes with greater frequency or severity than expected may have a material
negative impact on the ZIC Group’s business, financial condition and results of operations. This can be
exacerbated if the ZIC Group faces challenges to obtain optimal reinsurance protection (due to hard markets
with increasing capacity constraints and reinsurance rates).

The ZIC Group could also incur large losses from its Property and Casualty insurance business due to man-
made catastrophes such as cyber, terrorist attacks, or industrial accidents. In recent years, there has been an
increased incidence of reported cyber-attacks, including attacks allegedly committed by or on behalf of states
as part of hybrid warfare. Cyber-attacks can result in substantial financial losses from business interruption as
well as reputational damage, and an attack on one business or system may have wide reaching consequences
for others which rely on, or are connected with, it. An increase in the frequency or severity of cyber-attacks, as
well as changes in the regulatory environment could therefore expose the ZIC Group to substantially increased
liabilities under its policies, with adverse effects on its business, financial condition and results of operations.
In addition, the ZIC Group may be exposed to large losses from terrorist attacks to the extent that such events
may be only partially excluded from insurance coverage. Exclusions in coverage could also be challenged in
the event of doubt as to whether a particular incident can be clearly categorised as terrorism. Similar risks may
also exist in respect of the interpretation of exclusions for war.

to recession. See also “—Market Risks—Inflation Risk”. An unexpected increase in expenses may have an
adverse effect on the ZIC Group’s business, financial condition and results of operations.

Insurance Risk Related to Life Insurance
Insurance risks in the ZIC Group’s Life insurance business segment include mortality, disability, morbidity, and
longevity risks. Mortality, disability, and morbidity risks are associated with an unexpected increase in the
occurrence of death, disability, or medical claims under life or health insurance policies. Longevity risk is the
risk that the reserves covering life annuities and group pension products might not be sufficient due to longer
life expectancies of the insured. To the extent that actual claims in respect of any of these risks deviate in any
material respect from the assumptions that the ZIC Group used for the purposes of pricing and reserving Life
insurance business, it could have a material adverse effect on the ZIC Group’s business, financial condition and
results of operations. The long-term, often guaranteed, nature of Life insurance business exacerbates insurance
risk because the longer the product term, the more scope there is for experience to be different from what was
assumed at the time of pricing.

The assumptions that the ZIC Group makes in assessing its Life insurance reserves are prepared using “best
estimate” actuarial practices. The assumptions, derived from information provided from the ZIC Group’s
assessments, industry statistics and market information, relate to various matters such as mortality and
morbidity rates, long-term interest rates, investment returns and policyholder surrenders and future expense
levels. The ZIC Group continues to monitor and, if appropriate, adjust these assumptions in light of actual

experience and results. The assumptions the ZIC Group makes in assessing its Life insurance reserves may

Surrenders

Surrenders of deferred annuities and life insurance products can result in losses if surrender levels differ
significantly from assumed levels. Surrenders on certain Life products can require the ZIC Group to pay out a
current cash value of the surrendered policy, which could in turn lead to the ZIC Group, for the purposes of
raising funds to make that payment on surrender, to dispose of assets earlier than planned, possibly at a loss
especially if involving early redemption of large illiquid assets. Any such losses on disposal could have a
material adverse effect on the ZIC Group’s business, financial condition and results of operations.
Fee Business
On certain Life insurance products, such as unit-linked business, the ZIC Group earns a management fee linked
to the value of the funds under management where the level of this fee income is subject to financial market
volatility (e.g., changes to equity and bond prices and interest rates). Adverse market movements might reduce
the level of such management fees and thereby potentially reduce the ZIC Group’s capacity to cover expenses
and the cost of insurance, which in turn could have a material adverse effect on the ZIC Group’s business,
financial condition and results of operations.
Options and Guarantees

Some life products contain financial options and guarantees for policyholders, such as guaranteed interest rates
and surrender guarantees, meaning the ZIC Group guarantees a minimum value on maturity or surrender. These
vary by product and country in which they have been written. Adverse financial market movements may result
in increases in the value of these guarantees. The long-term characteristic of the liabilities associated with the

Stable Value Protection Features

Bank-owned life insurance products that contain stable value protection features (“SVPs”) are designed to
reduce the volatility of the policyholders’ returns from the portfolio into which their premiums are invested.
These products may have a policy life in excess of 40 years. In the event that a policy is surrendered which has
a positive SVP value, meaning that the policy value is higher than the value of the underlying portfolio, the
policyholder would be entitled to recover such SVP value as well as the market value of the underlying
investments. If the number of policy holders to surrender policies with a positive SVP value is higher than the
ZIC Group anticipates, it could have a material adverse effect on the ZIC Group’s business, financial condition
and results of operations.

Interest Rate Risks
Interest rate risk is the risk of an adverse economic impact resulting from changes in interest rates such as
changes in the shape of yield curves or a parallel shift in that curve. This risk may adversely affect the ZIC
Group’s assets, particularly the valuation of its portfolio of fixed-income securities, which comprises a
substantial portion of the ZIC Group’s total investments, the valuation of its liabilities in its Property and
Casualty and Life insurance business and the amount of capital that it is required to hold for regulatory solvency
purposes.

Any significant change in interest rates could have an adverse impact on the ZIC Group’s bond and interest rate
derivative positions and the value of liabilities. Increases in interest rates, as witnessed in recent years as central
banks in many major economies sought to control rising inflation, may result in a decrease in the fair market
value of the fixed-income assets held by the ZIC Group. See also “—Credit Spread Risk” and “—Inflation Risk”
below. Moreover, while an increase in interest rates should reduce the value of its liabilities from an economic
perspective, there may be mismatches in the ZIC Group’s asset and liability positions in terms of their respective
sensitivity to interest rate fluctuations.

In relation to the ZIC Group’s Life business, changes in interest rates resulting in reductions in the effective
investment income below the rates prevailing at the issue date of the policy, or below the long-term guarantees
in countries such as Germany and Switzerland, would reduce the profit margins or lead to losses on the Life
insurance business written by the ZIC Group’s Life subsidiaries to the extent the maturity composition of the
assets does not match the maturity composition of the insurance obligations they are backing. Moreover,
increases in prevailing interest rates may lead to a higher volume of surrenders of business in force.

Accordingly, any material change in interest rates may have a negative impact on the economic and regulatory
capitalisation of the ZIC Group.

The interest rate risks described above may have an adverse effect on the ZIC Group’s business, financial
condition and results of operations.

Credit Spread Risk
Credit spread risk arises from volatility in the difference in the yield between two securities of the same tenor
with different credit quality; most commonly one of the two securities is credit risk free, or considered as such
in financial markets (e.g., highest rated government bonds). The ZIC Group holds a significant portfolio of
fixed-income assets. The value of this portfolio is subject to fluctuations in response to movements in credit
spreads, in particular, the valuation of the portfolio may decrease if credit spreads widen. Credit spreads
typically widen at times of a perceived increase in risk by investors in the bond markets, such as for example
in response to heightened geopolitical tensions or deteriorating macroeconomic conditions. As a result, any
such changes in credit spreads could have a negative impact on the ZIC Group’s assets, financial condition and
results of operations, and, in addition, the value of assets ultimately realised by the ZIC Group may be materially
different from the current or estimated fair value.

Real Estate Risk and Other Alternative Investment Risk
The ZIC Group’s investment portfolio also includes real estate and alternative investments including private
debt, private equity, hedge funds, renewable energy and infrastructure investments. These investments are
subject to volatility in real estate, equity and alternative investment markets affecting the market value and
liquidity of these holdings. Debt investments are reviewed regularly and assessed for significant increases in
credit risk and credit impairment, with expected credit losses and any resulting impairment allowances
recognised in the ZIC Group’s profit or loss, together with changes in the fair value of equity investments.
Adverse changes in the value of real estate or other alternative investments could have a material adverse effect
on the ZIC Group’s financial condition and results of operations.

Inflation Risk
Ongoing macroeconomic and political developments could contribute to a resurgence in inflation. See “Other

the ZIC Group’s reserve position could also be negatively affected by inflation, particularly if inflation increases
or is subject to volatility to a greater extent as compared with the corresponding assumptions used for the
purposes of estimating reserves.

In relation to the ZIC Group’s Property and Casualty business, inflation causes increases in both claims and
expenses, such as, for example, inflation-driven increases in the costs of motor and property repairs, leading to
greater liabilities and payments to policyholders. If these increases in costs exceed the levels that the ZIC Group
anticipated when setting premium levels, the ZIC Group could incur underwriting losses.

Continuing high inflation has the potential to increase non-Life insurance liabilities further, in particular for
long-tail business where persisting inflation may adversely impact costs beyond current expectations. The
insurance market is also experiencing elevated levels of social inflation, the rising cost of insurance claims
resulting from societal trends and changes in legal environments (increased litigation, higher jury awards,
expansive interpretations of insurance coverage, and legislative changes that broaden liability). Social inflation
has outpaced economic inflation for many years, and contributes to higher loss costs and can significantly
impact the profitability and pricing of insurance products. The ZIC Group is also exposed to inflation risks in
its Life business due to, for example, obligations under life and health insurance contracts.

As the ZIC Group’s calculation of reserves includes assumptions about future payments for settlement of claims
and claims-handling expenses, the ZIC Group would be required to increase its loss reserves to the extent
inflation causes these costs to increase above established reserves, which could have a material adverse effect
on its business, financial condition and results of operations.

Climate Change Risk
Changes are expected in the frequency, severity and geographical distribution of extreme weather events, such
as tropical cyclones and extreme rainfall and associated flooding or heat waves as global temperatures rise. The
ZIC Group is exposed to physical risk of climate change through its underwriting. Changes in frequency and
severity of events caused by climate change add to the challenges in accurately measuring expected impacts.
As commercial catastrophe models are typically based on historical data and hence backward-looking, they
might not sufficiently account for climate risks already materializing. There is also a risk that physical events
reduce the profitability of investments across asset classes. A failure by the ZIC Group to adequately manage
its exposure to the physical risks of climate change could result in a material adverse effect on its business,
financial condition and results of operations.

In addition to these physical risks, the technological and policy changes required to achieve a transition to a
low-carbon economy in response to climate change create their own sets of risks. The transition, which most
likely would involve fundamental changes to all parts of the economy, could be disruptive, as significant asset
price moves may be required to shift resources to low-carbon technology on a global scale. Changes in public
perception and the regulatory landscape could reshape legal and reputational risks, and further uncertainties
may arise to the extent there is increased popular or governmental opposition in major economies to climate
change transition policies. The ZIC Group could be exposed to transition risks if it fails to manage changing
market conditions and customer needs as part of the transition to a low-carbon economy, resulting in asset
impairment, opportunity cost and lost market share. In a transition scenario, industries unable to decarbonise
could experience declining profitability and lack of re-financing, which could lead to a lack of maintenance
with increasing rates of outages and equipment breakdowns that translate into higher insurance losses. Failure
to manage transition risk could also lead to reputational impacts, both internal and external, resulting from a
failure to deliver on publicly stated commitments. In addition, the increasing frequency of climate-related legal
action indicates that climate-related litigation could represent a significant potential risk in the long term. A
failure by the ZIC Group to adequately manage its exposure to the transitional risks of climate change could
result in a material adverse effect on its business, financial condition and results of operations.

The Insurance Industry is Cyclical
The insurance industry has historically been subject to fluctuations in the volume of supply and pricing,
comprising periods of increased competition on premium rates and policy terms due to an excess of
underwriting capacity (a “soft” market) and periods when higher losses lead to more favourable pricing and
terms (a “hard” market).

Moreover, the ZIC Group’s Property and Casualty and Life insurance businesses may be subject to their own
distinct cycles, which may also be affected in turn both by changes to the composition of business written within
each segment and cyclicality within such business lines themselves. The financial impact on the ZIC Group of
a significant decrease in premium rates would be exacerbated by a trend towards higher loss costs resulting, for
example, from inflation-driven increases in labour and material costs or the costs of medical care in respect of
worker injury policies, which could impact the ZIC Group’s Property and Casualty business. Moreover, the ZIC
Group may be unable to increase premium rates in response to higher coverage costs due to regulatory or
competitive constraints and, as a result, profit margins on new or existing business could decline. In addition,
the ZIC Group transfers exposure to certain risks to third parties through reinsurance arrangements. The
availability, terms of, amount and cost of reinsurance are subject to significant variations depending on general

engineering and email compromise attacks exploiting human vulnerabilities now surpassing traditional malware
in prevalence. External actors—potentially including state-sponsored groups—continue to target organisations

and access management.

A successful cyber-attack on the ZIC Group, its vendors, or its supply chain could result in significant business
interruption, loss or corruption of data (including personal, confidential, or proprietary information), regulatory

of digital ecosystems means that an attack on one business or system may have cascading effects on others,
amplifying the risk of operational disruptions across the ZIC Group and its customers.

The regulatory environment governing cyber risk is complex and stringent. The ZIC Group is subject to a wide
range of laws, rules, and regulations related to cyber security and data protection, including the EU’s Digital
Operational Resilience Act (“DORA”), the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Swiss Federal
Data Protection Act and Information Security Act, as well as evolving requirements in other jurisdictions where
the ZIC Group operates. DORA, for example, introduces enhanced requirements for risk management, incident
reporting, resilience testing, and third-party risk oversight within the financial sector. Failure to comply with
these and other applicable regulations could lead to substantial regulatory fines, increased oversight,
reputational harm, or restrictions on business activities.

No system or process fully eliminates cyber risk. The risk of a material cyber-attack remains heightened,
particularly as digital transformation accelerates, cloud adoption increases, and threat actors adapt their
techniques. The ZIC Group expends significant resources to respond to or recover from cyber incidents,
investigate vulnerabilities, and comply with new regulatory obligations. A large-scale cyber-attack could have

Regulatory or Legal Changes

The ZIC Group operates in a highly regulated environment and is subject to supervision by regulators and
administrative authorities in all countries in which it operates as well as to group supervision in Switzerland.
Regulatory or administrative authorities have far-reaching powers addressing many aspects of the insurance
and financial services business, and insurance laws, regulations and policies currently governing the ZIC Group

In Switzerland, the main legislation regulating the operations of insurance companies comprises the Federal
Act on the Supervision of Insurance Companies (Bundesgesetz betreffend die Aufsicht über
Versicherungsunternehmen – Versicherungsaufsichtsgesetz, VAG) of 17 December 2004, as amended from time
to time (the “Insurance Supervision Act” or “ISA”). A partial amendment of the ISA came into force in 2024,
which introduced rules regarding the restructuring of insurance companies, as well as special conduct rules and
information duties as regards the sale of certain insurance-based investment products. Some of these changes
have started to lead to, and additional legislative amendments in the future may lead to, higher compliance and
legal costs as well as the possibility of higher operational, capital and liquidity costs. See also “—Insurance is
subject to Wide-Ranging Regulation”, “Risks Relating to the Subordinated Notes” and “Risks Relating to the
Market Generally”.

In the United States, state regulation is currently the primary form of insurance regulation as the federal
government does not directly regulate the business of insurance. However, federal legislation and administrative
policies can significantly affect insurance companies across various areas including financial services and
securities regulation (such as the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act in 2010),
pension regulation, privacy, tort reform legislation and taxation. The ZIC Group cannot predict what regulatory
proposals might be made in the future (and, if made, whether such proposals will be adopted) nor can it predict
what impact, if any, such proposals or, if enacted, such laws, could have on the ZIC Group’s business, financial
condition or results of operations.

At international level, following the 2008 financial crisis, a number of reforms of the regulation and supervision
of financial institutions and markets have been proposed by regulators, governments, groups thereof (such as
the G20 and its “post-financial crisis reform agenda”) and international bodies such as the Financial Stability
Board (“FSB”) which aim primarily at promoting financial stability and targeting the perceived gaps in the
regulatory and supervisory frameworks including possible changes in capital and liquidity requirements, and
complexity of groups including their structures. Improvements to the supervision of internationally active
insurance groups (“IAIGs”) is a key objective in this context. In this regard, the International Association of
Insurance Supervisors (“IAIS”), an association of insurance supervisors and regulators and a member of the
FSB, adopted in 2019 a Common Framework for the Supervision of Internationally Active Insurance Groups

(“ComFrame”), which provides a global framework of standards for IAIGs, including a risk-based, group-
wide global insurance capital standard (“ICS”), and a process for supervisors to cooperate in the supervision of
IAIGs. The IAS adopted the ICS at the end of 2024, and the implementation of the ICS by IAIS member
jurisdictions is underway. In addition, beginning in 2020, the IAIS implemented a holistic framework for the

Regulatory Capital Requirements

In each country in which the ZIC Group operates, the local regulator specifies the minimum amount and type
of capital that each of its regulated entities must hold in addition to their liabilities. In Switzerland, risk-based
capital requirements are regulated in accordance with the Swiss Solvency Test (the “SST”) as set forth in the
Ordinance on the Supervision of Private Insurance Companies (Verordnung über die Beaufsichtigung von
privaten Versicherungsunternehmen — Aufsichtsverordnung, AVO) of 9 November 2005, as amended from time
to time (the “Insurance Supervision Ordinance” or “ISO”) of 9 November 2005, as amended from time to
time, and the Ordinance on the Supervision of Private Insurance Companies of the Swiss Financial Market
Supervisory Authority FINMA (“FINMA”) (Verordnung der FINMA über die Beaufsichtigung von privaten
Versicherungsunternehmen — Versicherungsaufsichtsverordnung FINMA, AVO-FINMA) of 26 June 2024, as
amended from time to time. Swiss insurers are required to hold sufficient risk-bearing capital in order to cover
the required target capital under the SST. The ISO furthermore requires supervised entities to conduct their Own
Risk and Solvency Assessment and public disclosure requirements.

In this regard, ZIC uses its own FINMA-approved internal model for such purposes, as do the ZIC Group’s
other regulated Swiss entities (with the exception of Zurich Life Insurance Company Limited, which uses the
FINMA standard model). Since FINMA has authority to require adjustments to these models or the use of
standard models rather than internal models, these entities may be required to increase their capital based on

any such newly adjusted or standard model. The ZIC Group’s regulated entities in the European Union and the
United Kingdom are subject to similar economic risk-based solvency requirements under the Solvency II regime
and its UK equivalent. In the United States, the National Association of Insurance Commissioners periodically
considers and adopts revisions to the methodology for calculating the risk-based capital (“RBC”) ratios of
insurance companies, and is currently performing a holistic review of its RBC framework. Any revisions to
RBC resulting from such review or otherwise may increase the amount of capital and reserves insurance
companies are required to hold.

Tied assets regime in Switzerland may affect ZIC’s ability to comply with its obligations under or in
connection with the Notes or with its obligations under the ZIC Senior Guarantee or the ZIC
Subordinated Guarantee, as the case may be

In Switzerland, the claims of policyholders and insured persons are protected by the tied asset regime. A key
task of FINMA is to safeguard the claims of policyholders and insured persons against the consequences of
insurance undertakings becoming bankrupt. In order to be able to satisfy the claims of its policyholders and
insured persons, ZIC is required to set aside a sufficient level of insurance-related technical provisions
(versicherungstechnische Rückstellungen) calculated on the basis of actuarial principles. These technical
provisions must be covered at all times by restricted assets, the so-called tied assets (gebundenes Vermögen),
which are segregated from ZIC’s other assets.

Accordingly, ZIC is required to secure claims under insurance contracts with tied assets. The required target
amount of tied assets is equal to the insurance-related technical provisions plus an appropriate surcharge.

Tied assets are assets that are subject to legal restrictions or other requirements such that the tied assets cannot
be transferred without the prior consent of FINMA. In the event of bankruptcy, any proceeds from the sale of
tied assets will be applied first to claims under insurance contracts. Policyholders and insured persons will have
priority over other creditors (including, without limitation, Noteholders) because, in the event of bankruptcy,
claims of policyholders and insured persons will be paid from the proceeds of the sale of the tied assets and
such claims will be satisfied before those of any other creditor.

The ISA permits FINMA to order the allocation of ZIC’s assets to its tied assets up to the target amount (i) prior
to the occurrence of a Solvency Event, (ii) outside and independently of any Restructuring Proceedings in
respect of ZIC or (iii) upon the opening of or during any such Restructuring Proceedings. In any case, FINMA
has the power to and may order such allocation before an Event of Default or a Solvency Event, as the case
may be, has occurred, as well as at the same time or thereafter. See “Certain Aspects of the Swiss Resolution
Regime” and the risk factors “FINMA may order Swiss Protective Measures, open Restructuring Proceedings
(and exercise Swiss Resolution Powers in connection therewith) or institute bankruptcy proceedings with
respect to ZIC or ZIG irrespective of the occurrence of any Solvency Event” and “FINMA may order Swiss
Protective Measures with respect to ZIC or ZIG irrespective of any Restructuring Proceedings” for further
details.

Therefore, there is a preferred treatment of policyholders and insured persons and a preferred ranking of their
claims arising from insurance contracts. Tied assets cannot be used for settlement of obligations to other
creditors. This could affect ZIC’s position under the Notes and/or the ZIC Senior Guarantee or the ZIC
Subordinated Guarantee (as applicable) either in its capacity as Guarantor or as Issuer (as applicable).

FATCA Withholding
Certain provisions of U.S. tax law (commonly referred to as “FATCA”) generally impose a withholding tax of
30 per cent. on interest income (including Original Issue Discount (“OID”)) from debt obligations of U.S.
issuers such as ZHCA paid to a foreign financial institution (other than with respect to interest (including OID)
that is effectively connected with the conduct of a trade or business within the United States), unless such
institution either (i) enters into an agreement with the U.S. government to collect and provide to the U.S. tax
authorities substantial information regarding U.S. account holders of such institution (which would include
certain account holders that are foreign entities with U.S. owners) or (ii) in the event that an applicable
intergovernmental agreement and implementing legislation are adopted, complies with modified requirements
including in some cases providing local revenue authorities with similar account holder information. The
FATCA provisions also generally impose a withholding tax of 30 per cent. on interest income from such
obligations paid to a non-financial foreign entity (other than with respect to interest that is effectively connected
with the conduct of a trade or business within the United States) unless such entity provides the withholding
agent with a certification that it does not have any substantial U.S. owners or a certification identifying the
direct and indirect substantial U.S. owners of the entity or unless certain exceptions apply or they agree to
provide certain information to other revenue authorities for transmittal to the U.S. Internal Revenue Service
(the “IRS”).

Proposed Treasury Regulations provide that no FATCA withholding will be required with respect to payments
of gross proceeds on the disposition of obligations of a U.S. issuer. The preamble to these proposed Treasury
Regulations specifies that taxpayers are permitted to rely on the proposed Treasury Regulations pending
finalisation.

FATCA provisions also impose a 30 per cent. U.S. withholding tax on certain “pass-thru” payments by foreign
financial institutions. Proposed Treasury Regulations provide that the withholding tax will not be imposed on
pass-thru payments by foreign financial institutions before the date that is two years after the date of publication
in the Federal Register of final regulations defining the term “foreign passthru payment”.

Although the application of the FATCA withholding tax to pass-thru payments by foreign financial institutions
is still uncertain, as the scope of these rules are still being determined by U.S. tax authorities, it is possible that
in some circumstances payments by ZF (Australia), ZF (Ireland), ZF (Ireland) II or ZIC on Notes after the date
that is two years after the date of publication in the Federal Register of final regulations defining the term
“foreign passthru payment” to persons failing to meet certain FATCA reporting or certification requirements
may be treated as “pass-thru payments” subject to U.S. withholding tax. Such withholding would apply to a
Note characterised as debt (or which are not otherwise characterised as equity and have a fixed term) for U.S.
federal tax purposes that are issued or deemed issued after the date that is six months after the date on which

final U.S. Treasury Regulations defining the term “foreign passthru payment” are filed with the Federal

EU Anti-Tax Avoidance Directives
As part of its anti-tax avoidance package, the European Commission published a draft Anti-Tax Avoidance
Directive on 28 January 2016, which was formally adopted by the European Council on 12 July 2016 in Council
Directive (EU) 2016/1164 (the “ATAD 1”). The ATAD 1 was to generally be implemented by each Member
State by 2019, subject to certain derogations for Member States which have equivalent measures in their
domestic law. Ireland introduced the ATAD 1 interest limitation rule (see below) pursuant to the Finance Act
2021 in respect of accounting periods occurring on or after 1 January 2022.

The second Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (the “ATAD 2”, and, together with ATAD 1, the “ATADs”) was
adopted as Council Directive (EU) 2017/952 on 29 May 2017. ATAD 2 was to be implemented by all EU
member states by 1 January 2020, with certain exceptions in the case of measures relating to reverse hybrid
mismatches which were implemented by Ireland from 1 January 2022. The ATADs may affect the tax treatment
of an Issuer’s profits and therefore an Issuer’s ability to make payments on the Notes.

Amongst the measures contained in the ATAD 1 is an interest deductibility limitation rule similar to the
recommendation contained in the Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Action 4 proposals. The ATAD 1 provides
that interest costs in excess of 30 per cent. of an entity’s earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and
amortisation, are not deductible in the year in which they are incurred but remain available for carrying forward
(while Member States also have the option of excluding the first €3,000,000 of interest costs). However, the
restriction on interest deductibility is only in respect of the amount by which the borrowing costs exceed
“interest revenues and other equivalent taxable revenues from financial assets”. So long as the Issuers generally
fund the interest payments each makes under the Notes from interest payments to which each is entitled on the
refinancing of existing debt of the Zurich Insurance Group (that is such that each of the Issuers pays limited or
no net interest), the restriction should be of limited relevance to the Issuers.

ATAD 1 (as amended by ATAD 2) provides for hybrid mismatch rules. These rules have applied in Ireland since
1 January 2020 and are designed to neutralise arrangements where amounts are deductible from the income of
one entity but are not taxable for another, or the same amounts are deductible for two entities. These rules could
potentially apply to ZF (Ireland) and/or ZF (Ireland) II where: (i) the interest that either pays under the Notes,
and claims deductions from its taxable income for, is not brought into account as taxable income by the relevant
Noteholder, either because of the characterisation of the Notes, or the payments made under them, or because
of the nature of the Noteholder itself; and (ii) the mismatch arises between associated enterprises, between ZF
(Ireland) and/or ZF (Ireland) II and an associated enterprise or under a structured arrangement.

The measures should not impact payments on the Notes where ZF (Ireland) and/or ZF (Ireland) II has or had at
any time an associated enterprise that holds Notes unless there is a hybrid mismatch.

For the purposes of the hybrid rules, a structured arrangement is one involving a mismatch outcome where the
mismatch outcome is priced into the terms of the arrangement or the arrangement was designed to give rise to
a mismatch outcome. While it is unlikely that ZF (Ireland) or ZF (Ireland) II would be entering into structured
arrangements, revenue guidance indicates that in determining whether there is a structured arrangement, the
issue is whether a hypothetical reasonable entity would be expected to have knowledge that it entered into a

structured arrangement, that it shared in the value of the tax benefit and that any mismatch arising has not been

The market continues to develop in relation to risk-free rates (including SARON and SOFR) as
reference rates for floating rate Notes
The Rate of Interest for a Series of Floating Rate Notes or Fixed to Floating Rate Notes may be determined by
reference to the daily Swiss Average Rate Overnight (“SARON”) (any such Notes, “SARON-Linked Notes”),
which is the alternative to CHF LIBOR (which ceased to be published after its last publication on 31 December
2021) recommended by the National Working Group on Swiss Franc Reference Rates. The Rate of Interest may
also be determined by reference to the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (“SOFR”) (any such Notes, “SOFR-
Linked Notes”). In each such case, investors should carefully consider the below when making their investment
decision with respect to any such Notes.

Investors in SARON-Linked Notes or SOFR-Linked Notes should be aware that the market continues to
develop in relation to SARON or SOFR as a reference rate in the lending and capital markets and its adoption
as an alternative to CHF LIBOR and USD LIBOR, respectively. The market or a significant part thereof may
adopt an application of SARON or SOFR as a reference rate that differs significantly from that set out in the
Conditions and used in relation to SARON-Linked Notes or SOFR-Linked Notes, as applicable. The
development of SARON or SOFR as a reference rate, as well as continued development of SARON-based rates
or SOFR-based rates for such markets and the market infrastructure for adopting such rates, could result in
reduced liquidity or increased volatility or could otherwise affect the market price of SARON-Linked Notes or
SOFR-Linked Notes.




                                                    38

This relates not only to the substance of the calculation and the development and adoption of market
infrastructure for the issuance and trading of Notes referencing such rates, but also how widely such rates and
methodologies might be adopted.
The Rate of Interest applicable to each Interest Accrual Period for SARON-Linked Notes will be determined
on the basis of SARON Compounded, while that of SOFR-Linked Notes will be determined on the basis of
Compounded Daily SOFR or Compounded SOFR Index. This means that the Rate of Interest applicable to each
such Interest Accrual Period will only be capable of being determined shortly before the end of such Interest
Period. Consequently, it may be difficult for investors in SARON-Linked Notes or SOFR-Linked Notes to
estimate reliably the amount of interest that will be payable on such Notes on each Interest Payment Date, and
some investors may be unable or unwilling to trade such Notes without changes to their information technology
systems, both of which could adversely impact the liquidity of such Notes. Further, if any SARON-Linked
Notes become due and payable on a date other than an Interest Payment Date (whether as a result of an Event
of Default or redemption or otherwise), the Rate of Interest applicable to the final Interest Accrual Period will
only be determined based on SARON for each Zurich Banking Day during the related SARON Observation
Period to the date on which such Notes become due and payable, rather than for the entire SARON Observation
Period. If any SOFR-Linked Notes become due and payable on a date other than an Interest Payment Date, such
Interest Accrual Period will end on (but exclude) such date on which such Notes become due and payable.

In addition, the manner of adoption or application of SARON or SOFR reference rates in the debt capital
markets may differ materially when compared with the application and adoption of SARON or SOFR in other
markets, such as the derivatives and loan markets. Investors should carefully consider how any mismatch
between the adoption of SARON or SOFR reference rates across these markets may impact any hedging or
other financial arrangements, if any, which they may put in place in connection with any SARON-Linked Notes
or SOFR-Linked Notes.

Since SARON and SOFR are relatively new market indices, SARON-Linked Notes or SOFR-Linked Notes
may have no established trading market when issued, and an established trading market may never develop or
may not be very liquid. Market terms for debt securities indexed to or referencing SARON or SOFR, such as
the spread over the index reflected in interest rate provisions, may evolve over time, and trading prices of such
debt securities may be lower than those of later issued indexed debt securities as a result. Further, if SARON or
SOFR does not prove to be widely used in securities like SARON-Linked Notes or SOFR-Linked Notes, the
trading price of such Notes may be lower than those of debt securities linked to indices that are more widely
used. Investors in SARON-Linked Notes or SOFR-Linked Notes may not be able to sell such Notes at all or
may not be able to sell such Notes at prices that will provide them with a yield comparable to similar investments
that have a developed secondary market, and may consequently suffer from increased pricing volatility and
market risk. There can also be no guarantee that SARON or SOFR will not be discontinued or fundamentally
altered in a manner that is materially adverse to the interests of investors in SARON-Linked Notes or SOFR-
Linked Notes. If the manner in which SARON or SOFR is calculated is changed, that change may result in a
reduction of the amount of interest payable on SARON-Linked Notes or SOFR-Linked Notes and the trading
prices of such Notes.

The Rate of Interest applicable to each Interest Accrual Period for SARON-Linked Notes will be determined

The regulation and reform of “benchmarks” may adversely affect the value of Notes linked to or
referencing such “benchmarks”
Reference rates and indices, including interest rate benchmarks, such as the Eurozone Interbank Offered Rate
(“EURIBOR”), which are used to determine the amounts payable under financial instruments or the value of
such financial instruments, have been the subject of political and regulatory scrutiny as to how they are created
and operated. This resulted in regulatory reform and changes to existing “benchmarks”. Most reforms have now
reached their planned conclusion and benchmarks remain subject to ongoing monitoring. These reforms and
changes may cause a “benchmark” to perform differently than it has done in the past or to be discontinued. Any
change in the performance of a “benchmark” or its discontinuation, could have a material adverse effect on any
Notes referencing or linked to such “benchmark”. The EU Benchmarks Regulation was published in the Official
Journal of the EU on 29 June 2016 and applied from 1 January 2018. The EU Benchmarks Regulation applies
to the provision of in-scope benchmarks, the contribution of input data to an in-scope benchmark and the use
of an in-scope benchmark within the EU. It, among other things, (i) requires benchmark administrators to be
authorised or registered (or, if non-EU-based, to be subject to an equivalent regime or otherwise recognised or
endorsed) and (ii) prevents certain uses by EU supervised entities of in-scope benchmarks of administrators
that are not authorised or registered (or, if non-EU based, not deemed equivalent or recognised or endorsed).
Regulation (EU) 2016/1011 as it forms part of domestic law by virtue of the EUWA (the “UK Benchmarks
Regulation”), among other things, applies to the provision of benchmarks and the use of a benchmark in the
UK. It prohibits the use in the UK by UK supervised entities of benchmarks of administrators that are not
authorised by the UK Financial Conduct Authority (the “FCA”) or registered on the FCA register (or, if non-
UK based, not deemed equivalent or recognised or endorsed).

The EU Benchmarks Regulation and/or the UK Benchmarks Regulation, as applicable, could have a material
impact on any Notes linked to or referencing a “benchmark” which is in-scope of one or both regulations, in

particular, if the methodology or other terms of the “benchmark” are changed in order to comply with the
requirements of the EU Benchmarks Regulation and/or the UK Benchmarks Regulation, as applicable. Such
changes could, among other things, have the effect of reducing, increasing or otherwise affecting the volatility
of the published rate or level of the “benchmark”.

More broadly, any of the international or national reforms, or the general increased regulatory scrutiny of
“benchmarks”, could increase the costs and risks of administering or otherwise participating in the setting of a
“benchmark” and complying with any such regulations or requirements. Such factors may have the following
effects on certain “benchmarks”: (i) discourage market participants from continuing to administer or contribute
to the “benchmark”; (ii) trigger changes in the rules or methodologies used in the “benchmark” or (iii) lead to
the disappearance of the “benchmark”. Any of the above changes or any other consequential changes as a result
of international or national reforms or other initiatives or investigations, could have a material adverse effect
on the value of and return on any Notes linked to or referencing a “benchmark”.

Investors should consult their own independent advisers and make their own assessment about the potential
risks imposed by the EU Benchmarks Regulation and/or the UK Benchmarks Regulation reforms in making
any investment decision with respect to any Notes linked to or referencing a “benchmark”.

           secured and/or pre-funded to its satisfaction), take action to enforce the obligations of the Issuer in respect
           of such unpaid principal or interest provided that the Trustee and the Noteholders have no right to claim
           any sums in respect of or enforce an early redemption of the Notes or institute proceedings for the winding-
           up of the Issuer.

    (b)    No institution of winding-up proceedings

           satisfaction) participate in, but not itself institute, any proceedings for the winding-up of the Issuer to
           enforce the obligations of the Issuer for payment of any principal or interest (including any Arrears of
           Interest) in respect of the Notes.

           right conferred on them, to file for the opening of bankruptcy proceedings (Konkursbegehren) with respect
           to the Issuer or other winding-up proceedings or to make other similar filings or motions which, if
           approved, would lead to a redemption of the Notes.

    that the net amounts received by the holders of the Notes after such withholding or deduction shall equal the

    shall be payable with respect to any Note presented for payment:

CERTAIN ASPECTS OF THE SWISS RESOLUTION REGIME

Capitalised terms used but not defined in this section shall have the meaning given to them in the ZIC
Subordinated Notes Conditions and the Guaranteed Subordinated Notes Conditions, as applicable.

General

In Switzerland, insurance companies supervised by FINMA (such as ZIC) and Swiss-domiciled parent companies
of insurance groups supervised by FINMA (such as ZIG) are, among others, subject to the Insurance Supervision
Act and the ordinances promulgated thereunder.

With effect from 1 January 2024, the Insurance Supervision Act was partially amended (for further details see
“Risk Factors — Regulatory or legal changes”). In connection with this revision, parts of the resolution regime
applicable to ZIC and ZIG have been amended. The resolution regime under the amended Insurance Supervision
Act contains rules that may be relevant for the Notes, the ZIC Senior Guarantee, the ZIC Subordinated Guarantee,
any Relevant On-Loans, the Trustee, the Noteholders and/or other creditors of ZIC and ZIG. In particular, it
permits FINMA to adopt the Swiss Protective Measures and the Swiss Resolution Powers under certain
circumstances. Against that background, the following overview is intended to provide a summary of the Swiss
Protective Measures and the Swiss Resolution Powers. It is provided for information purposes only and does not
claim to be exhaustive.

Swiss Protective Measures

FINMA may order Swiss Protective Measures (i) if, and to the extent necessary to safeguard the interests of
insured persons, (1) ZIC or ZIG, as the case may be, fails to comply with Swiss insurance supervisory laws and
regulations or with FINMA orders or (2) the interests of insured persons otherwise appear to be jeopardised, or
(ii) if there are reasonable grounds for concern that ZIC or ZIG, as the case may be, is over-indebted or has
serious liquidity problems. Thus, the Insurance Supervision Act permits FINMA to order Swiss Protective
Measures with respect to ZIC and/or ZIG (i) prior to the occurrence of a Solvency Event, (ii) outside and
independently of any Restructuring Proceedings or (iii) upon the opening of or during any Restructuring
Proceedings.

Swiss Protective Measures may include (i) prohibiting the free disposal of assets, (ii) ordering the deposit or
freezing of assets, (iii) transferring all or part of the powers vested in the governing bodies to a third party, (iv)
transferring the insurance portfolio and the associated tied assets to another insurance undertaking with the latter’s
consent, (v) ordering the realisation of tied assets, (vi) demanding the dismissal of the persons entrusted with the
ultimate direction, supervision, control or management or of the general agent(s) and the responsible actuary and
prohibiting them from exercising any further insurance activity for a maximum of five years, (vii) ordering the
allocation of assets of an insurance undertaking to its tied assets up to the target amount, and/or (viii) ordering a
stay (Stundung) or deferral (Fälligkeitsaufschub) of payments such as payments by ZIC under the Notes, the ZIC
Senior Guarantee, the ZIC Subordinated Guarantee and/or any Relevant On-Loan, as the case may be.

Under certain conditions, ZIC or ZIG, as the case may be, may challenge the Swiss Protective Measures ordered
by FINMA against it in a competent Swiss court. Any person other than ZIC or ZIG, respectively, such as the
Noteholders or the Trustee may not be entitled to reject, or seek the suspension of, the Swiss Protective Measures
or challenge the imposition of any such Swiss Protective Measures in a Swiss court.




                                                     239

Swiss Resolution Powers

If FINMA concludes that there are reasonable grounds for concern that ZIC or ZIG, as the case may be, is over-
indebted or has serious liquidity problems, FINMA may, in addition to the adoption of Swiss Protective Measures,
open Restructuring Proceedings (and exercising any Swiss Resolution Powers in connection therewith) or
institute bankruptcy proceedings with respect to ZIC or ZIG, as the case may be, after FINMA has first allocated
assets of ZIC to its tied assets up to the target amount.

If FINMA opens Restructuring Proceedings with respect to ZIC or ZIG, as the case may be, FINMA will have the
discretion to exercise its Swiss Resolution Powers, which include the power to (i) transfer ZIC’s insurance portfolio,
or portions thereof, together with tied assets, debt and other liabilities, or portions thereof, and insurance contracts,
to another insurance undertaking, (ii) stay (for a maximum of two business days) the termination of contracts to
which ZIC or ZIG, as the case may be, is a party, and/or the exercise of rights to terminate, netting rights, rights
to enforce or dispose of certain types of collateral or rights to transfer claims, liabilities or certain collateral under
contracts to which ZIC or ZIG is a party, (iii) stay (for a maximum of four months or, if a restructuring plan is
approved by FINMA, two months after such approval) the termination of reinsurance contracts to which ZIC is a
party, and/or the exercise of termination rights thereunder, and/or (iv) partially or fully convert into equity of ZIC or
ZIG, as the case may be, or write-down the liabilities of ZIC or ZIG, as the case may be, including obligations under
or with respect to the Notes, the ZIC Senior Guarantee, the ZIC Subordinated Guarantee and/or any Relevant On-
Loans, as applicable.

In Restructuring Proceedings, the Noteholders, the Trustee and/or other creditors of ZIC or ZIG, as the case may
be, may only vote on any restructuring plan approved by FINMA pursuant to which it exercises such Swiss
Resolution Powers if the relevant restructuring plan restricts the rights of the creditors of ZIC or ZIG, as the case
may be. If at least half of all known creditors of ZIC or ZIG, as the case may be, reject the restructuring plan in
such a vote, FINMA will institute bankruptcy proceedings with respect to ZIC or ZIG, respectively.

Noteholders, the Trustee and/or other creditors of ZIC or ZIG may only challenge FINMA’s approval of the
restructuring plan in Swiss courts in general, but not the individual Swiss Resolution Powers imposed thereby.
Additionally, the upholding of such appeal by a Swiss court will not result in the revocation of the restructuring
plan, but in compensation for the respective appellant (e.g. in the form of shares or other participation rights in ZIC
or ZIG, as the case may be).
